title: The Birthday Problem: When 23 people Are Enough
teaser: A surprising probability problem showing that in a group of just 23 people, there is a greater than 50% chance that at least two people share the same birthday.
author: Nour Al-Zahraa Karnib
level: Basic understanding of fractions, multiplication, and probability is helpful, but no advanced mathematics is required.
refs: 1. Wolfram MathWorld — Birthday Problem at https://mathworld.wolfram.com/BirthdayProblem.html | David Aldous, UC Berkeley — STAT 134: Concepts of Probability at https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/134/index.html | Diaconis & Mosteller — Methods for Studying Coincidences at https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous /157/Papers/diaconis_mosteller.pdf | R Documentation — Probability of Coincidences at https://www.stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/birthday.html

title: What the Planes Didn't Show
teaser: A surprising story about statistician Abraham Wald and how studying the damage on surviving airplanes led to a completely different conclusion about where protection was needed. The anecdote introduces the idea of survivorship bias and shows why missing data can be just as important as the data we can see.
author: Nour Al-Zahraa Karnib
level: Basic understanding of statistics, probability, and simple data interpretation is helpful. No advanced mathematics is required
refs: Abraham Wald — A Reprint of “A Method of Estimating Plane Vulnerability Based on Damage of Survivors” | Center for Naval Analyses — Wald's 1943 work | Marc Mangel & Francisco J. Samaniego — “Abraham Wald's Work on Aircraft Survivability” | Journal of the American Statistical Association, 79(386), 259–267 (1984). | Journal article — Taylor & Francis | American Statistical Association — Abraham Wald's work and statistical history | American Statistical Association — Abraham Wald | Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics — discussion of Wald's aircraft-survivability example | SIAM — Everyday Problems “Shot Through with Mathematics”

title: The Road That Made Everyone Slower!
teaser: Adding a new road can sometimes make traffic worse for everyone? The anecdote explores how individually rational choices can lead to an inefficient outcome for the whole system.
author: Nour Al-Zahraa Karnib
level: Basic algebra and an understanding of simple fractions and equations.
refs: Dietrich Braess (1968), “Über ein Paradoxon aus der Verkehrsplanung,” Unternehmensforschung, 12, 258–268. DOI: 10.1007/BF01918335. D. Braess, A. Nagurney, and T. Wakolbinger (2005), “On a Paradox of Traffic Planning,” Transportation Science, 39(4), 446–450. DOI: 10.1287/trsc.1050.0127. H. Youn, M. T. Gastner, and H. Jeong (2008), “Price of Anarchy in Transportation Networks: Efficiency and Optimality Control,” Physical Review Letters, 101, 128701. DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.101.128701.
